name: Scalp vibrator (vintage)

card.summary: An early-1900s electric or hand-powered vibrating scalp device sold through health-and-beauty advertising, aimed at the scalp and hair.
card.note: Historical device; documentation of specific hair claims is sparse.

quick.overview:
Vibrating scalp devices belong to the era when electric and hand-driven vibrators were sold for home health and beauty. Vibrators began as medical instruments in the late 1800s and from around 1900 were advertised in magazines with claims of health and beauty benefits, including use on the scalp.

For appearance the idea was scalp stimulation for hair and scalp condition. Little documentation survives of formal testing of these particular devices, and they are mostly known today through period advertising and collectors.
quick.how: Period vibrators were sold by mail order and in catalogs, including Sears, Roebuck, and applied by holding the vibrating head against the scalp, face or body for short sessions. They were electric or hand-powered.
quick.risks: No specific safety documentation was found for these devices. Early electrical appliances of the period varied in build, and the marketing claims of the era were broad.

lead: A vintage scalp vibrator is an early twentieth-century vibrating device used on the scalp. Electric vibrators were invented as medical instruments in the late nineteenth century for pain relief and a range of ailments, and were applied to the scalp for headaches, the skin for wrinkles and the stomach for indigestion.[1]

From about 1900 vibrators were advertised for home use in magazines and sold by mail order, by brands such as White Cross and through catalogs including Sears, Roebuck in 1918, with health and beauty claims.[1] An 1899 McClure's advertisement for the Vibratile offered a cure for neuralgia, headache and wrinkles.[1]
Devices aimed at the scalp for hair loss fit within this tradition. No published trials of these early devices were found, and modern scalp massage is a separate topic.[2]

chain: Vibrating head held against the scalp
Marketed as supporting hair and scalp health
angle.text: The devices were pitched to buyers as a way to stimulate the scalp for hair and scalp health. Advertising of the period made health and beauty claims for vibrators generally.

paras: The electromechanical vibrator is credited to physicians of the 1870s and 1880s; one account places first use at the Salpetriere hospital in Paris in 1878, and Joseph Mortimer Granville's 1883 book described uses for pain, neuralgia and digestion.[1]

Advertisements from about 1900 to 1920 promoted vibrators for health and beauty, and mail order was the standard sales method; the vibrators' marketing largely left respectable publications in the mid-1920s.[1]
Scalp massage is described generally as massage directed to the scalp or head, and handheld mechanical scalp massagers are sold today.[2]

timeline.event: Early reported clinical use of electric vibrators at Salpetriere.[1]
Vibratile advertisement in McClure's offers a cure for neuralgia, headache and wrinkles.[1]
Sears, Roebuck catalog sells vibrators by mail order.[1]
